Salesforce Content Experience 

@mention: Style Guidelines 

An @mention is the @ symbol followed by the name of a person or group, for example, @Maria Sanchez or @DocTeam.  

@Mentions are used in Slack posts and comments to tag people and groups. When you @mention a user or group, your post appears in that feed,  and the @mention links to the profile of the user or group. 

Capitalize @mention as you would other words. Use @Mention if it’s the first word in a sentence or part of a title. Otherwise, use  lowercase. 

You can use @mention as a verb a noun, or in plural form.  

| Example |
| :---- |
| @Mention users when sharing a file with groups.  In the Comments field, @mention users and groups.  The @mention links to the person’s profile. |

To ask a style question or to suggest a Style Guidelines or UI Text Standards update, post to \#cx-doc-style.

a, an: Style Guidelines 

Use a before words that start with a consonant or a “yew” sound. Use an before words that start with a vowel or a vowel sound. If an acronym is generally read as alphabetic letters, choose the article according to the sound of the first letter in US English:

abbreviations: Style Guidelines 

| ![][image2]abbreviations: Style Guidelines  Abbreviations include acronyms, shortened forms of terms, and symbols for units of measure. In general, abbreviate terms that are  repeated often or that must appear in tables or other tight spaces, but don't confuse your reader with too many abbreviations. When  in doubt, spell out the term. In most cases, don't abbreviate product or feature names.  See also: Best Practices for Optimizing Content for Generative AI |
| :---- |

General Rules 

The first time you use an acronym or abbreviation that isn't obvious, spell out the word or phrase and follow it with the shortened form in  parentheses. 

For example: A local area network (LAN). Use the acronym or abbreviation in all subsequent references. 

In long manuals or manuals that include sections that customers can read separately, it can be useful to readers to repeat the full name and  abbreviation the first time a term is used in each new topic. 

Don't use an apostrophe for plurals. For example, the plural of FAQ is FAQs, not FAQ's. 

Don't use periods with most acronyms or abbreviations for technical terms, standard nontechnical abbreviations, or abbreviations for units of  measure: 

ANSI (acronym)   
MB (technical abbreviation)   
PhD (nontechnical abbreviation)   
ft (unit of measure) 

Capitalization 

When spelling out an acronym, capitalize the individual words only if they're proper nouns. Use all capital letters for the acronym itself. In titles, don't alter the capitalization of file extensions or abbreviations. For examples, see capitalization of abbreviations, editions, file  extensions, code, cross-references: Style Guidelines. 

If an acronym is generally read as alphabetic letters, choose the article according to the first letter. For example: an API, a URL. 

Don't Spell Out Common Acronyms and Abbreviations  

Certain acronyms and abbreviations are so common that you never have to spell them out. However, if you're using a domain-specific  acronym, determine audience familiarity. If you feel the readers would benefit from it, expand and introduce the acronym at first mention. This  is especially true when you're setting the context in release notes for a new feature. 

Here's a list of acronyms we typically don't spell out.

Measurements and Units 

Don't use abbreviations like K for thousand or M or MM for million. Exception: K and M are acceptable for representing potentially  large numbers in the UI, for example number of views of a post. But ask the developer to mark the label as English only. If the abbreviations are common to the audience, it's acceptable to abbreviate measurements: for example, 100 KB; 1 GHz.

All images in documentation require alt text, which represents visual elements to blind or low-vision users. When writing alt text, be concise and  include only the information that's relevant.  

Best Practices 

Provide text that conveys the purpose and meaning (or function) of an image. Alt text is important for search engines because it makes content  more accessible. Search engines want to rank accessible content. It also improves topical relevance, can support image rankings and serves as  anchor text for image links. See Improve Help Topic SEO. 

Aim for one sentence. Try to keep the text at 150 characters or less.   
Treat alt text as you would any other user-facing text: Use sentence capitalization, proper grammar, and no end punctuation unless it’s a  complete sentence. 

Use accurate UI names in text.   
Consider the text before/after the image to reduce duplication.   
Avoid describing the image as an image: Rarely do you need to include image of, photo of, screenshot of, logo, icon, or graphic. However,  if any such words are necessary for context or clarity, it’s OK to include them. 

Write alt text in the same tone and voice as the surrounding text.   
For more complex images such as charts, consider either reproducing the data in a tabular format on the page or linking to a page  containing a longer description which fully describes the data represented.  

Avoid putting critical text-based instructions in an image including form data or steps. Instead, spell out this information in the  surrounding text as well as in the image. Low vision users may have trouble seeing the image and may not be able to access the alt text. 

Describe what the screenshot shows.   
Focus on the details relevant to the image's context.

When referring to a Salesforce API version, use the word version and include one decimal value after the whole number. Don't abbreviate version to v. When referring to any product before or after a given API or product version number, use earlier and later. Don't say before or after.

This object is available in API version 35.0 and later.

API Name: Style Guidelines 

In UI text, use API Name for the field that the admin sets when creating custom objects, custom fields, and any customization that requires a  unique name that an admin can reference from another customization. In docs, use API Name to refer to this field. 

A note on Unique Name and “Developer Name" 

While the value within the API Name field must always be unique, don't refer to an API name as the unique name or unique API name. 

In the API, the API Name field value is stored in a field called DeveloperName. Sometimes on older screens in the UI, you'll see Developer Name as  the label for the API Name field. Your teams probably call it developer name. But don’t use Developer Name as the label in the UI. 

Example of the API Name for a Custom Object 

When an admin creates a custom object, the Object Name field is automatically populated with the text from the admin-entered Label. Spaces and  special characters are replaced with underscores. The admin can edit the Object Name, but it has to follow naming conventions. 

When the admin saves the custom object, the API Name is automatically generated by adding “\_\_c” (that’s two underscores) to the Object  Name. The API then refers to the custom object by the API name.

Note: Standard objects also have an API Name field, but it’s not exposed in the application. 


Example of the API Name for a Custom Field 

Similarly, the API Name for a custom field is derived from the Field Name, appended with “\_\_c”. 

(Although in UI, it’s still called the Field Name.) 

Example of the API Name for a Flow 

Each flow element or resource, such as a variable, screen field, or text template, requires a unique name so that the flow admin can uniquely  reference that element or resource from another element or resource. The API Name field contains that unique name.  

When deriving the API Name value for a flow element or resource, the system replaces or removes spaces and special characters from the admin entered label but doesn’t append anything. 

The flow element below includes a label because that label is displayed on the flow canvas. Also, the decision element has nested outcomes, each  of which has its own label and API Name.

The flow resource doesn’t include label because it’s not displayed. 

UI Text for API Name field infobubbles 

We have standard infobubble text for API Name fields that outlines the requirements, with the caveat that sometimes the API Name rules can differ  in the various apps. 

The API Name can contain only underscores and alphanumeric characters. It must be unique, begin with a letter, not include spaces, not end with  an underscore, and not contain two consecutive underscores. 

Instructions and error messages 

When writing API Name-related instructional UI text and inline errors, use language that’s action-oriented and positive when possible.  Enter only alphanumeric characters and underscores. Don’t include special characters.

associate vs. relate: Style Guidelines 

The verbs associate and relate aren't interchangeable in a Salesforce context. 

Don't use associate to or associate with when referring to a relationship between objects. Use relate to instead. Customers can create  relationships to link objects with each other, so that when users view records, they can also see related data. 

On the other hand, an associated object is an object about another object. For example, for object XYZ there can be an associated object  called XYZHistory that contains historical data about changes to the fields on XYZ. 

Keep this usage in mind when creating feature or UI labels.

assure, ensure, insure: Style Guidelines 

These terms are often confused. 

Ensure means to make certain. Don't use assure to express this meaning. 

NOTE: Instead of ensure, say make sure; it sounds less stilted.   
Better yet, leave out make sure altogether, and lead with an imperative verb: 

OK: Make sure to check out your files, then click Next.   
BETTER: Check out your files, then click Next. 

Assure means to set someone's mind at rest. 

Insure means to indemnify against loss.

capitalization of abbreviations, editions, file extensions,  code, cross-references: Style Guidelines 

Abbreviations 

Retain the capitalization of abbreviations (for example, 1-kHz Oscillator, Start Sync at 12:00 AM), even in titles. Editions 

Capitalize both words in an edition name, as in Enterprise Edition and Group Edition. Don't capitalize edition when it appears by itself as a  common noun: Accounts are available in all editions. 

File Extensions 

Use all lowercase when you name file extensions. Word adds .docx to a file name if you don't specify the file format when saving. Use all caps to mention a file type such as CSV or PDF. Export the data as a CSV file.  

Code 

In titles, retain the case of objects, calls, methods, SOAP headers, and any code element, such as `create()`. If a sentence begins with a  code element, consider rewriting so that the element isn't the first word. 

After a Colon 

Capitalize the first word after a colon only when the clause is a complete sentence or formal quotation. For example: Don't forget this point:  The report is due by 9:00. 

Cross-References 

Use all lowercase when commonly referring to elements of a document in general and uppercase when referring to a specific figure, table,  appendix, or chapter. 

This table shows...   
This section covers...   
See Figure 6 for an illustration...   
See Chapter 3, Chapter Name   
See Table 3, Common Fault Codes 

Use all lowercase when commonly referring to elements of a document in general and uppercase when referring to a specific figure, table,  appendix, or chapter. 

Don’t capitalize the words page, step, line, or column, even when they're followed by a number: 

See pages 4–5.   
Refer to step 14\.   
See column 2\.

title capitalization: Style Guidelines 

Use title capitalization in titles and headings—including definition list titles and column headings in tables—and as specified in the UI text  standards. 

Words to Capitalize 

When title capitalization is required, capitalize these words. 

Nouns (Switcher, Migration), including nouns used to modify other nouns (Validation Rules, Verification Methods) Adjectives (Encrypted, Multiple) 

Pronouns (It, That, You, Your, Who, Which; more examples) 

Verbs (Is, Are, Deliver, Encrypt) 

All words in a verb phrase (Turn On, Sign In, Log Out; more examples) 

Adverbs (Easily, Quickly) 

Prepositions five or more letters long (Without, Between; more examples) 

The first and last words of a title, no matter what the words are 

The first word after the colon in a title (for example, Flexible Pages: The Big Picture) 

Words in hyphenated compounds (for example, Real-Time Quotes, Third-Party Software, Two-Factor Authentication; but Just-in-Time  Manufacturing) 

Key names like Ctrl, Alt, Del (don't use all caps) 

Subordinating conjunctions (Although, Because, If, When; more examples) 

Words Not to Capitalize 

When title capitalization is required, don't capitalize these words. 

Articles (a, an, the) and coordinating conjunctions (and, but, for, no, or, so, yet) 

The to in an infinitive (to Be) 

Prepositions that have fewer than five letters (examples; to, with, from) and are not part of a verb like Sign In   
See Also

Title Case Converter

click: Style Guidelines 

All references to mouse clicks assume that the user has configured the left mouse button as the primary mouse button and the right one as the  secondary. 

Click means click the left mouse button.   
Right-click means click the right mouse button.   
Double-click means click the left mouse button twice.   
Don’t use click on. Do use: Click Merge to finish.   
Don’t use click, use tap when describing gestures users perform in a mobile app with a touchscreen interface.  Don't use click into. Do use: Click in the Search field. 

Don't use Click Save. Toward universal help content, use: Save your changes. Save your work.

When introducing large amounts of code, avoid naming the type of code if possible. For example, don't introduce a code sample written in Java as t his Java or the following Java. When you can't avoid using a term to introduce a code sample, use the following terms, depending on what the  sample is. 

Apex script   
Apex class   
Apex trigger   
Visualforce markup 

You can also specify the language in a heading, such as Java Sample or C\# Sample. Use this in a reference guide when you are presenting more  than one version of a program, class, or method. 

Using XML or HTML is acceptable in the context of The following HTML contains Visualforce markup. 

Use four spaces when indenting code samples, when possible. Spaces must be consistent within a sample and across a topic. Use sentence capitalization for code block titles in SFDocs. 

For more code sample guidelines, see Sample Code Guidelines. 

Use ALL CAPS for SOQL keywords such as SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, AND, OR, and LIMIT.   
Capitalize field names as they appear in the API. Use camel case starting with a capital letter. For example, BillingCity.

| :---- |
| SELECT Id, Name FROM Account WHERE Name='Acme' LIMIT 1 |

| Tag  | Description |
| ----- | :---- |
| \<code  block\> | Use `<codeblock>` for a block of code one line or longer, such as sample Java code used in the API, sample Apex code, or a sample  formula. |
| \<code  ph\> | Use `<codeph>` for code-related words or phrases that are less than a line long. Code-related words or phrases include formulas,  functions, constants, API calls, Apex classes, methods, and triggers. For a block of code or code that exceeds one line, use the `<codebl ock>` tag. |
| \<parm  name\> | Use `<parmname>` for all fields that represent fields on an object, including picklist names. Keep in mind that not all fields in the UI  represent fields on an object. Also, use `<parmname>` for API call parameter names, except in Apex documentation, where you use `<varn ame>` instead. |
